title: What this is, and what it isn't
summary: A plain-language look at the four moves of the workbook and the things it does not promise.
body:
## Four moves

You do not need a business idea, a passion, or a personal story to start. The workbook is built around four moves: Notice, Try, Reflect, Decide. You notice something. You try a small step if you want to. You think about how it went. Then you decide what is next. Each move is small, and you can take them in your own time.

## More than one way forward

The group listens, asks questions, and gives feedback when you ask for it. People do not all end up in the same place. A job, training, a project, a pause, a new direction, or still looking all count. Starting a business is one option. It is not the goal, and nobody is expected to pick it.

## What it isn't

This is not therapy, treatment, or diagnosis. It is not a readiness test. It does not promise a job, income, recovery, or business success. You do not have to explain your history to belong here. You can pause or leave at any time. Saving a short note is not the same as sharing it with anyone.

> Imagined example: Someone reads this page and saves one line: "This program does not promise me a job. I want to know what support is available." That line holds one thing the page said and one question. It needs no life story.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Five separate choices
summary: Joining is not agreeing to everything: each choice stands alone and you can say no to any of them.
body:
## A yes to one is not a yes to all

These five choices are separate. Taking part: coming to sessions and doing activities. Evaluation: giving feedback on how the program is working. Recording: audio, video, or photos. Story or publicity use: your words or image used to talk about the program. Follow-up: being contacted after the program. If you say yes to one, you have not said yes to the others. Any new use of your words or image needs a new ask.

## What you can always do

You can choose what you share. You can pass on any question. You can ask who can see what is stored about you. You can ask for a correction. You can raise a concern. You never need to share addiction, legal, medical, or diagnostic history to take part. If you need something practical, you can ask for it without saying why.

## Privacy has limits

Staff cannot promise that everyone in the group will keep what you say to themselves. Share with that in mind. On this site, check how answers are stored and what sharing sends before you enter anything sensitive. On a shared or public device, other people may be able to see what you enter. This page explains your choices. It is not the consent form.

> Imagined example: Someone comes to every session. They say yes to evaluation feedback, no to recording, and not now to story use. Each choice stands on its own, and they can change any of them later.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: The Group Code in plain words
summary: Ask first, stay on the work, be specific, keep things private, and help without rescuing.
body:
## Ask first

The Group Code is a short set of ground rules for working together. It is not a pledge. Before giving advice, ask: "Would you like a question, a suggestion, or no feedback right now?" If the answer is no or not now, stop there. A "no" does not need a reason, and a group vote can never take away anyone's right to pass or keep something private.

## Stay on the work and be specific

Being okay to talk about one piece of work does not mean being okay to talk about someone's life. Be specific. "The instructions don't say how long it takes" is something you can check. "You never think things through" is a judgment about a person. Talk about actions, not identities or diagnoses.

## Keep it private, help without rescuing

Do not repeat someone's story, record them, or take photos without their permission. Offer only support you can actually give. Helping is not policing or monitoring. Accountability partners are separate and optional. [ASHLEY: add the confirmed concern contact if a boundary gets crossed.]

> Imagined example: Someone has sketched a layout for a shared supply shelf. A peer asks, "Would you like a question, a suggestion, or no feedback right now?" The person says, "A question." The peer asks, "What should people find first?" The person takes the idea, leaves it, or changes it.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Your support plan, in your words
summary: A short note on what helps you show up, with no reasons or history needed.
body:
## What a support plan is

A support plan is a short note on what helps you show up. It is not a test of commitment. It is not a medical history or a consent form. Every part is optional, and you can change it anytime. "Nothing to add right now" is a complete answer if it is true.

## Things to think about

How you like to take part: speaking, writing, working privately, or watching. Access: reading or language support, hearing or vision, seating, mobility, breaks. Tech: shared device, phone only, limited data. Life logistics: childcare, transport, work shifts, your schedule. You do not need to cover every one.

## Describe the need, not the reason

Say what you need, not why. "I can read on my phone, but I need paper for longer writing" is enough. No diagnosis or history is needed. A request starts a conversation. It is not a promise that the program already offers it. [ASHLEY: name the role or person who handles support requests.]

> Imagined example: "Writing privately. Paper handouts, please. Phone only, limited data. I work Saturdays. No extra support for now. Starting question: I don't know yet."
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Joining is about now
summary: Choosing to join is not a promise to finish, and the seven decision words are used all through the program.
body:
## A choice for now

Choosing to join is about now. It is not a promise to finish everything. You can start, ask questions, change how you take part, pause, or decide it is not the right time. If something is unclear, that is on the program to explain better. It is not a failed test. [ASHLEY: add how someone tells the program they are pausing or leaving.]

## Joining is separate from other choices

Joining does not include evaluation, recording, story use, or follow-up. Each of those is its own Yes, No, or Not now. You do not need to explain a no. "I will watch first and decide after the session" is a real decision.

## Seven decision words

You will see the same seven words at the end of every step. Keep: continue what is useful. Change: adjust your approach. Test again: gather more information. Pause: set it aside for now. Stop: end this activity or direction. Another direction: turn toward something else. Keep looking: leave the question open. None is better than another.

> Imagined example: "I'll join with adjustments: paper handouts, and I'll observe the first session."
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: A map of the week you actually have
summary: Your Life Map is a picture of right now, with five areas and no scoring.
body:
## Not an ideal schedule

Your Life Map is a picture of the life you are living now. It is not an ideal schedule or a picture of who you should become. It links what interests you with where, when, and how things really work. You do not have to fill every area. One line is a fine start, and empty spots tell you something too.

## Five areas

Places: where things happen, and whether you can get there, feel welcome, and afford it. Activities anywhere: reading, walking, talking, making, fixing, helping. Energy: what left you steadier, and what took more than it gave. Barriers: cost, transport, childcare, access, schedules, credentials. Threads: questions or activities you keep coming back to.

## Two facts can both be true

"I liked the library workshop, but it is at night when I work" holds two facts: an interest and a scheduling barrier. Neither cancels the other. A barrier is a condition, not a character flaw. You choose which journal entries, if any, to link. Nothing is scored.

> Imagined example: Places: the community kitchen, two bus rides away; the library, a ten-minute walk. Energy: steadier after making something, drained after a day of meetings. No conclusions yet, just what is true.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Describe first, decide later
summary: Notice what held your attention, keep what happened separate from what it might mean, and let "I don't know yet" count.
body:
## Start small

You do not need a passion, a career choice, or a business idea to begin. Start with something small: a question you keep returning to, something you looked into, or an ordinary task you finished or avoided. Ask which part held your attention. Ask which part felt hard, annoying, or worth another look. If nothing stands out, "nothing clear yet" is a complete result.

## Curiosity, enjoyment, commitment

These three are different. Curiosity means you want to know more. Enjoyment means you liked some part of the experience. Commitment means choosing to keep giving it time or effort. One does not require the next. You might enjoy comparing options but not doing the task. You might avoid something because the instructions were unclear, not because it does not interest you.

## What happened, and what it might mean

Write what happened before you decide what it means. "I watched two repair videos" is an observation. "I should become a mechanic" is a possible interpretation. Two videos do not establish it. Leave what you do not know marked as unknown. You can put both parts in one note, as two kinds of information and not two required entries.

> Imagined example: Someone spends twenty minutes comparing three ways to repair a loose drawer handle. What happened: they compared the tools and steps each method needed. What held their attention: a fix that used tools they already had. What they chose not to do: buy anything or start the repair. What is unknown: whether they would enjoy the repair, or just wanted the drawer fixed.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Two patterns, not two kinds of people
summary: A way to notice how an activity fits into your life, without labeling yourself.
body:
## The useful question

An activity can matter deeply and still leave room for the rest of life. It can also become pressured or hard to put down. The useful question is not "Am I an obsessive person?" It is "How is my relationship with this activity working in this situation?" The answer can change from one day or one place to another.

## Two patterns

An obsessive pattern involves pressure, rigidity, or feeling controlled by the activity. Stopping may feel hard, and self-worth may get tied to continuing or performing. A harmonious pattern involves chosen, flexible engagement. The activity matters, but there is room to stop, adapt, and attend to other responsibilities. Harmonious does not mean easy, mild, or always enjoyable.

## What to notice

Notice choice, flexibility, pressure, energy, and the ability to pause. Notice how it fits with health, rest, relationships, responsibilities, and support. Conditions around the activity matter too. These are patterns, not types of people, diagnoses, or scores. Mixed and unclear are valid descriptions. One observation does not establish a pattern.

> Imagined example (not a participant story): Two evenings spent on the same drawing project. On one, someone picks a stopping point and returns later. On another, they keep going because stopping feels like proof of failure, even though they wanted to protect a responsibility. The activity looks similar. The relationship to it differs. Neither evening gives anyone a label.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Plan one small try before you do it
summary: Pick something to learn from, check the real conditions, and write the limit and stop rule first.
body:
## Any starting point works

You can begin with something that already interests you, or with no clear candidate. Both work. A thread might be a task, a field, a question, a practical problem, or something you would like to understand. The aim is not to find a permanent passion. It is to gather one piece of information that helps your next choice. "Not this" is useful information too.

## Check the real conditions

Look at money, transport, schedules, childcare, technology, housing, accessibility, energy, and support. An option that needs transport you do not have is not a test of your motivation. Choose something accessible, make it smaller, or record the barrier. Observing, sampling, or planning can be enough for now. No purchase, public performance, or business idea is required.

## Write the plan first

If you plan to try something, write down what you hope to learn and the smallest real action. Add how much time, money, and energy you will use. Add who or what could help, and what signal means you stop or adjust. Then pick when you will look back. These can go in one note. They do not need eight separate answers. Bring earlier notes only if you choose to.

> Imagined example: Someone has no clear candidate. They choose between watching a repair demonstration, sorting a set of materials, or asking one person how a task works. They pick a ten-minute option, stop at the agreed end, and write whether anything felt more or less worth looking into.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: A short evidence check, not an essay about you
summary: Keep what you did, what you saw, what you think it means, the conditions, and the cost in separate lines.
body:
## Reflection is a short check

Reflection asks what happened, under which conditions, what it took, and what is still unknown. A few specific details help more than a broad verdict about yourself. An observation is something you saw, did, or can check. An interpretation is what you think it means. "I stopped after ten minutes because the instructions would not load" is an observation. "I am not interested enough" is an interpretation the observation does not show.

## Conditions and cost

Include the setup: time available, instructions, access, support, interruptions, or unfamiliar tools. Include the cost: effort, tiredness, money, and any help you needed afterward. Enjoying something and finding it workable are different questions, and both can be mixed. Boredom, friction, no access, no opportunity, and uncertainty belong in the record. A blocked try tells you about a barrier.

## Do not invent a result

"I did not get a chance to find out" is more accurate than a made-up result. One try can inform your next question. It cannot settle ability, readiness, belonging, or long-term fit. If you share your account, keep it separate from someone else's explanation. Ask permission before suggesting a pattern in another person's work, and accept correction.

> Imagined example, not a participant story. Report: "I followed the instructions for ten minutes." Observation: the checklist was done in order. Interpretation: "the person likes structured work." Conditions: quiet room, written instructions. Cost: needed more time, no money spent. Unknown: whether the same holds in a different setting.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)

title: Review, then choose what is next
summary: Compare what you expected with what happened, then pick a Next Decision. None is better than another.
body:
## A review is not a test

A review helps you decide what to do with what you learned. It is not a graduation test, and you do not need a positive result to finish. Start by comparing what you expected with what happened. Include the conditions and after-effects. A task might have held your attention but left little energy for something important. Those lead to different questions, not to a single success or failure.

## Next Decision words

Keep: something worth continuing. Change: an adjustment. Test again: another observation would help. Pause: set it aside for now. Stop: end it. Another direction: turn toward something else. Keep looking: leave the question open. Pause and Stop protect the option not to continue. No word is better than another. Choose the one that fits what the evidence says.

## Honest unknowns and what you carry

"The task interested me, but the session was too long" names evidence and an adjustment. "Access was blocked; I do not know whether I like it" keeps an honest unknown. A useful try is not proof of destiny or readiness. You choose what to carry forward and what stays private. Optional ratings, if you use them, are only tools for noticing and are never a cutoff or a ranking.

> Imagined example: A short exposure was interesting at first but needed more time and support than expected. The record might say: change the conditions, test once more with a shorter task, and stop if the cost stays too high.
source_label: Learning pack v0.1 (AI-drafted companion reading, pending Ashley review)
